The first International Conference on Health Promotion, meeting in Ottawa this 2Ist day of
November 1986, hereby presents this CHARTER for action to achieve Health For All by the year 2000

and beyond.

This conference was primarily a response to growing expectations for a new public health movement
around the world. Discussions focused on the needs in industrialized countries, but took into account
similar concerns in all other regions.It built on the progress made through the Declaration of Primary
Health Care at Alma Ata, the World Health Organization’s Targets for Health For All document, and
the recent debate at the World Health Assembly on intersectoral action for health.

HEALTH PROMOTION

Health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their
health. To reach a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, an individual or group
must be able to identify and to realize aspirations, to satisfy needs, and to change or cope with the
environment. Health is, therefore, seen as a resource for everyday life, not the objective of living.
Health is a positive concept emphasizing social and personal resources, as well as physical capacities.
Therefore, health promotion is not just the responsibility of the health sector, but goes beyond healthy
life-styles to well-being.

PREREQUISITES FOR HEALTH

The fundamental conditions and resources for health are peace, shelter, education, food, income, a
stable eco-system, sustainable resources, social justice and equity. Improvement in health requires a
secure foundation in these basic prerequisites.

ADVOCATE

Good health is a major resource for social, economic and personal development and an important
dimension of quality of life. Political, economic, social, cultural, environmental, behavioural and
biological factors can all favour health or be harmful to it. Health promotion action aims at making
these conditions favourable through advocacy for health.

ENABLE

Health promotion focuses on achieving equity in health. Health promotion action aims at reducing
differences in current health status and ensuring equal opportunities and resources to enable all people
to achieve their fullest health potential. This includes a secure foundation in a supportive environment,
access to information, life skills and opportunities for making healthy choices. People cannot achieve
their fullest health potential unless they are able to take control of those things which determine their
health. This must apply equally to women and men.

MEDIATE
The prerequisites and prospects for health cannot be ensured by the health sector alone. More
importantly, health promotion demands coordinated action by all concerned: by governments, by
health and other social and economic sectors, by non-governmental and voluntary organizations, by
local authorities, by industry and by the media. People in all walks of life are involved as individuals,
families and communities. Professional and social groups and health personnel have a major responsi-
bility to mediate between differing interests in society for the pursuit of health.
Health promotion strategies and programmes should be adapted to the local needs and possibilities
of individual countries and regions to take into account differing social, cultural and economic
systems.

COMMITMENT TO HEALTH PROMOTION

The participants in this conference pledge:

© to move into the arena of healthy public policy, and to advocate a clear political commitment to

health and equity in all sectors;

to counteract the pressures towards harmful products, resource depletion, unhealthy living con-

ditions and environments, and bad nutrition; and to focus attention on public health issues such as

pollution, occupational hazards, housing and settlements;

© to respond to the health gap within and between societies, and to tackle the inequities in health
produced by the rules and practices of these societies;

* to acknowledge people as the main health resource; to support and enable them to keep themselves,
their families and friends healthy through financial and other means, and to accept the community
as the essential voice in matters of its health, living conditions and well-being;

* to reorient health services and their resources towards the promotion of health; and to share power
with other sectors, other disciplines and most importantly with people themselves;

® to recognize health and its maintenance as a major social investment and challenge; and to address
the overall ecological issue of our ways of living.

The conference urges all concerned to join them in their commitment to a strong public health
alliance.

The European Health Data Space (EHDS) is a health-specific and 
governance framework designed for sharing health data across 
borders within the European Union, establishing clear rules, common 
standards, and practices along with digital infrastructures like 
MyHealth@EU and HealthData@EU aiming to improving healthcare.
The three main objectives of EHDS are to:
1 empower individuals to take control of their health data and facilitate 
the exchange of data for the delivery of healthcare across the EU 
(primary use of data);
2 provide a consistent, trustworthy, and efficient system for reusing 
health data for research, innovation, policy-making, and regulatory 
activities (secondary use of data
3 foster a genuine single market for electronic health record systems 
(EHR systems).

Accepted: 26 August 2022 / Published online: 13 September 2022
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2022

I suggest defining Precision Public Health as a concept of using effective, fair,
and reliable data and social enterprise to improve the health of all and, especially
the most marginalized populations. The specific requirements—to be effective. fair,
and reliable—are driven by data credentials and analytical tools provided by and to
public health professionals and ethical standards for inclusiveness and transparency.
Our ability to recognize what human factors or the social enterprise means in the
current conditions will define whether Precision Public Health is here to stay.

As we define Precision Public Health as a concept of using effective, fair, and
reliable data-rich social enterprise, we expand its most common description as the
right imervention to the right population at the right time by emphasizing the lasting
public health’s historical ideals of improving the well-being of all with human-
centered decision making.

lernziele.text: Mission und Arbeitsweise von Public Health beschreiben.
Health in All Policies und gesundheitsfördernde Stadtplanung erklären.
Chancen und Risiken von Digital Public Health, KI und Precision Public Health benennen.

kernaussagen.text: Die MedUni Wien ist seit 2004 eigenständig (vorher Medizinische Fakultät der Universität Wien); die Folien stellen Kliniken, Bauprojekte, Universitätsleitung und Studienangebot vor.

Mission von Public Health: Bedingungen sichern, unter denen Menschen gesund sein können (Institute of Medicine 1988); kollektives Handeln für nachhaltige Gesundheitsverbesserung der ganzen Bevölkerung (Beaglehole et al. 2004).
Public-Health-Interventionen wirken in komplexen Systemen, die sich nicht vollständig kennen, steuern oder vorhersagen lassen.
Prävention zielt letztlich auf die „5 Ds“: Death, Disease, Disability, Discomfort, Dissatisfaction (Fletcher 2009).
Individuen und Krankheiten existieren nicht außerhalb ihres sozialen, politischen, historischen und geografischen Kontexts (Walker et al. 2023).

Public-Health-Interventionen nutzen ein breites Spektrum: Policies, Gesetze, Regulierung, Organisations- und Gemeindeentwicklung, Bildung, Technik, Dienstleistungen, Kommunikation und Social Marketing (Rychetnik et al. 2004); Politikgestaltung hängt von wissenschaftlichen, ökonomischen, sozialen und politischen Kräften ab.

abschnitte.titel: Health in All Policies, Gesundheitsförderung und Stadtplanung

kernaussagen.text: Health in All Policies wird über die GÖG-Plattform hiap.goeg.at vorgestellt; die Ottawa-Charta (1986) steht für den Gesundheitsförderungsansatz.

WHO Healthy Urban Planning: zwölf Ziele, u. a. gesunder Lebensstil und Bewegung, sozialer Zusammenhalt, guter Wohnraum, Zugang zu Arbeit und Einrichtungen, gesunde Lebensmittel, Sicherheit, Chancengerechtigkeit, gute Luft und wenig Lärm, Klimaschutz (Barton et al. 2011).
Die „Settlement Health Map“ (Barton et al. 2011) hebt vulnerable Gruppen in der Stadtplanung hervor: Ältere, Kinder, junge Eltern, Frauen, Ärmere, Arbeitslose, immobile Personen.

abschnitte.titel: Digital Public Health und Künstliche Intelligenz

kernaussagen.text: Digitale Transformation (Health 4.0) bindet Menschen stärker in ihr Gesundheitsmanagement ein; maßgeblich ist dabei Gesundheitskompetenz.

Der European Health Data Space (EHDS) ist ein Rahmen für den grenzüberschreitenden Austausch von Gesundheitsdaten in der EU mit gemeinsamen Regeln, Standards und Infrastrukturen (MyHealth@EU, HealthData@EU).
KI kann sechs Kernfunktionen von Public Health unterstützen: Gesundheitsförderung, Surveillance, Gesundheitsschutz, Population Health Assessment, Prävention, Krisenvorsorge (Fisher et al. 2022).

Neue Datenquellen (soziale Medien, Apps, Wearables, Umweltsensoren) liefern laufend Informationen zu sozialen, verhaltensbezogenen und Umweltdeterminanten und lassen sich mit klassischen Public-Health-Daten verknüpfen.
Der Einsatz von KI ist nie rein technisch: Er berührt Rechte, Chancen und Freiheit und verlangt Verantwortung, Transparenz und Governance.
Precision Public Health nutzt Genomik und Big Data für zielgenauere Public-Health-Maßnahmen und wirft ethische, rechtliche und soziale Fragen (ELSI) auf (Roberts et al. 2024).
Gender ist eine relationale Gesundheitsdeterminante, weil es den Blick auf alle sozialen Determinanten verändert (Keleher).
Gender wirkt als „verborgener Organisator“: Unterschiede in Mortalität und Morbidität zwischen Männern und Frauen entstehen aus Lebensbedingungen und Einkommen (Dierks 2008).
Der Europarat erarbeitete 2005–2006 Empfehlungen, die biologische, kulturelle und soziale Dimension von Gender in Public-Health-Programme und Ausbildung zu integrieren.
Brennpunkte der Frauengesundheit u. a. Kontrazeption, Migration, Schwangerschaftsabbruch, Fertilitätsbehandlung, Gender Gap bei der Arbeitszeit.
